title: Rook behind the passed pawn
summary: Tarrasch's rule: the rook belongs behind the passed pawn, yours and your opponent's.
part.own.title: Behind your own pawn
part.own.summary: The same pieces with the rooks swapped: behind wins, in front draws.
part.get.title: Getting behind
part.get.summary: Bringing the rook behind the pawn, and getting there before the enemy rook.
part.theirs.title: Behind the enemy pawn
part.theirs.summary: In defence the rook also goes behind the pawn; in front of it, the rook is tied down.
part.rules.title: Recap
part.rules.summary: Tarrasch's rule, the exception that cost Kramnik a game, and the practical challenge.
step.t_behind: You play White and have a passed pawn on the a-file. Look at where each rook stands. Can Black hold this pawn? And what is your plan to win?
step.t_behind.hint1: Compare the two rooks. How many squares does each have on the a-file, and how many will it have when the pawn advances?
step.t_behind.hint2: The black rook cannot leave the front of the pawn. So your king is the one who helps the pawn, and Black has only the king to defend both the pawn and the kingside.
step.behind: Your rook is behind the pawn, the black rook is in front of it. Look at the difference. With every step the pawn takes, your rook gains one more square on the file and keeps protecting the pawn. The black rook does the opposite: it loses squares. With the pawn on a7 it has only a8, and if it leaves, the pawn queens. One rook has become a guard; the other is free. This is the rule Siegbert Tarrasch wrote down more than a hundred years ago: the rook belongs behind the passed pawn.
step.front: Now the same pieces, with the rooks swapped. Your rook stands in front of the pawn and has nowhere to go: it blocks its own pawn. The black rook, behind it, attacks the pawn and checks your king from a distance if it tries to come closer. Black keeps the king on g7 or h7 and waits. And that is a draw. Same pieces, same side to move: only the rooks' placement changed the result.
step.d_walk: Watch how White wins the good position. The idea is simple: the black rook is tied down, so your king walks to the pawn.
step.d_walk.m1: 1.a7! The pawn advances and the black rook is pinned to a8. If it leaves the file, the pawn queens with your rook's protection.
step.d_walk.m2: The black king heads for the centre.
step.d_walk.m3: Your king sets off towards the pawn. No hurry: Black has nothing to do.
step.d_walk.m4: Black decides to guard the g6 pawn.
step.d_walk.m6: The black king can only wait.
step.d_walk.m8: Now the black king tries to come back to the queenside, but it is late.
step.d_walk.m9: The white king arrives first and controls b7.
step.d_walk.m10: The black king cannot step onto c7: the white king guards that square.
step.d_walk.m11: 6.Kb7 attacks the rook. It has to leave a8, and the pawn promotes with your rook's support. Notice that the white rook never had to move: behind the pawn, it works while standing still.
step.twoTargets: Now you play. Advance the pawn and bring the king to the centre. If the black king runs to the queenside, go and take the g6 pawn.
step.twoTargets.hint: 1.a7, then 2.Kf3, 3.Ke4, 4.Kf4 and 5.Kg5. The rook stays on the a-file.
step.twoTargets.done: The black king went to stop the a-pawn and abandoned the g-pawn. Two targets for one king. The black rook helps with neither, because it is stuck in front of the pawn.
step.t_side: The black rook attacks your pawn from the side. Only one move keeps the win. Which one?
step.t_side.hint1: Look for the square from which the rook protects the pawn and still gains room when it advances.
step.side: 1.Ra1. The rook goes behind the pawn: it protects the pawn and gains a square with every advance. To stop the pawn, the black rook will have to stand in front of it, tied down as in the previous position. Any other move loses the pawn and the win.
step.ra1: Bring the rook behind the pawn.
step.ra1.hint: Along the first rank, to the a-file.
step.ra1.done: Done: the rook is behind the pawn. Now it is the black rook that will have to blockade.
step.race: Sometimes the direct route is too slow. Here the white rook wants to get behind the pawn. If it goes via 1.Rc3, the black rook checks on f2 and next move goes to a2: it gets behind the pawn first, and then the good rook is Black's. The right move is 1.Rc2: it takes the second rank away from the black rook, and next move the white rook reaches a2.
step.getFirst: Your turn: get behind the pawn before the black rook does.
step.getFirst.hint: 1.Rc2, to close the second rank. Then 2.Ra2, and the king comes to the centre.
step.getFirst.done: Your rook got behind the pawn first. Now it is the position you already know: the black rook stuck in front of the pawn and your king free to walk.
step.t_defend: Now Black has the passed pawn and you defend. The a-pawn is protected by the black rook. Where should your rook go?
step.t_defend.hint1: Think of the rule you just saw. It works for both sides.
step.t_defend.hint2: Blockading the pawn looks safe, but look at what your rook would do there: nothing. Find the way to the square behind the pawn.
step.defend: The rook goes behind the pawn: 1.Rd8 and then 2.Ra8. From there it attacks the pawn, and the black rook has to keep protecting it. Every time the pawn advances, your rook gains squares and the black one, beside or in front of it, loses them. White also holds with the active rook on d5, d6 or with the check on d7. What loses is the blockade: 1.Ra1.
step.passive: See what happens after 1.Ra1. Your rook is in front of the pawn, tied to it: if it leaves, the pawn runs. The black rook is free, and the black king can walk to the pawn to push it. Black wins. A rook in front of the pawn is passive, whoever it belongs to.
step.holdBehind: Bring your rook behind the black pawn.
step.holdBehind.done: The rook is behind the pawn and attacks it. The pawn may advance, but with each step it gets further from the black rook that protects it and closer to yours, which attacks it. A draw.
step.tarrasch: Siegbert Tarrasch, one of the great German masters of the early twentieth century, wrote in the book of the St. Petersburg 1914 tournament that rooks belong behind passed pawns: behind your own to support the advance, behind the opponent's to hinder it. The reason is the one you have just seen: the rook behind gains room with every step of the pawn, the rook in front loses it.
step.except: But it is a rule, not a law. Tarrasch himself is quoted as saying: always put the rook behind the pawn, except when that is wrong. This position is from Kramnik against Beliavsky, 1993. Kramnik played 59.Ra1, behind his own pawn, and lost. There, 59.a4, 59.Rc1 or taking the rook to b6, b7 or b8 drew. The rule points the way; calculation confirms it.
step.recap: Three rules to take to your games. One: with a passed pawn, the rook goes behind it. Two: against the opponent's passed pawn, the rook also goes behind it; blockading with the rook is the passive defence. Three: getting behind the pawn is a race; before you go, check that the enemy rook does not get there first with a check.
step.finish: Now the practical challenge, from the position at the start of the lesson. Keep the rook behind the pawn, bring the king forward and win.
ex.e05: White to move and win. The black rook stands in front of the pawn. How do you exploit that?
ex.e05.hint: The white king wants to reach b7. What stops it right now?
ex.e05.solution: 1.Rb2+! The check drives the black king off the b-file. After 1...Ka6, 2.Kc7! and the white king reaches b7: the black rook, in front of the pawn, cannot guard a8 and give checks at the same time. Beware of 2.Kc6, which looks the same and only draws. Idea from SHREKDAVID's Lichess study.
ex.e06: White to move and win. Your rook is in front of the pawn, but the black king has left the right square. Punish the mistake.
ex.e06.hint: Free the a8 square with a threat. What happens if the black rook takes the pawn?
ex.e06.solution: 1.Rh8! It threatens 2.a8=Q. If the rook takes the pawn, 2.Rh7+ skewers king and rook along the seventh rank. With the black king on g7 or h7 this trick does not exist: that is why Black keeps the king there.
ex.e11: White to move and win. The rook is not behind the pawn yet, and the black rook is already eyeing a6. Where should your rook stand, and how does it get there in time?
ex.e11.hint: In front of the pawn the rook only draws. To get behind it you need a spare tempo. Who can give it to you?
ex.e11.solution: 1.Rc5+! The check gains the tempo, and next move 2.Ra5 puts the rook behind the pawn, guarding a6. Without the check, the black rook takes the pawn first. 1.Ra8, in front of it, only draws: after 2.a7 the black rook gets behind the pawn on the a-file and checks your king. Position from miles26's Lichess study.
ex.e10: White to move and win. Here the rule misleads: the rook behind the h-pawn only draws. Find the winning move.
ex.e10.hint: Your king is stuck in front of its own pawn. What stops the black king from coming closer?
ex.e10.solution: 70.Rf7! The rook cuts the black king off along the f-file, and the white king gets out of the pawn's way. 70.Rf6, 70.Rf1 and 70.Rf2 also win. In Short against Yusupov, 1984, White played 70.Rh3, behind the pawn, and the game was drawn.
ex.e12: White to move and draw. Each side has a passed pawn, and Black's is closer to queening. Only one move holds.
ex.e12.hint: Your rook has two jobs: helping your pawn and stopping the c-pawn. Which move keeps it free for the second one?
ex.e12.solution: 1.f6! The pawn advances on its own and the rook stays free on the h-file. If 1...c3, the rook goes to h8 and checks on d8, and gets behind the c-pawn. If 1...Rf5, then 2.Rf3. 1.Rf3 straight away, behind your own pawn, looks like Tarrasch's rule but loses: 1...c3, and the c-pawn runs while the white rook is tied to the f-file. From Audax6's Lichess study.
ex.e13: White to move and win. Yusupov against Timman, 1992. Your a-pawn is passed. Where does the rook work best?
ex.e13.hint: Behind the pawn the rook protects only one thing. Look for a square where it protects more than one pawn.
ex.e13.solution: 35.Re4! From the fourth rank the rook protects the a-pawn from the side and the f-pawn at the same time. The black rook stays tied to the a-pawn, and the white king is free to advance. 35.Ra1, behind the pawn, was the game move: the rook had only the a-pawn to look after, and the game was drawn twenty moves later. A Wikipedia example of an exception to the rule.
ex.e14: White to move and win. Unzicker against Lundin, 1954. The black rook is behind your pawn and the black king threatens to break into your kingside. Only one move wins.
ex.e14.hint: Pushing the pawn is the plan, but first think: after a check on a2, where would the black king go?
ex.e14.solution: 48.f3+! Only this move wins. The check drives the black king away from your kingside, and only then comes 49.a7. If 48.a7 at once, 48...Ra2+ and the black king gets to f3: it attacks your pawns and the defence holds. After 48.f3+ and 49.a7, the black rook can only watch the pawn, and the white king walks over to it. Wikipedia notes that with the black pawn still on f7 the king could go back to f6 or g7 and it would be a draw.
ex.e15: White to move and win. Your f-pawn is one step from queening, but the black rook is behind it. Think before you promote.
ex.e15.hint: The black rook holds the pawn only along the f-file. How can your rook cut that file?
ex.e15.solution: 1.Rb5! The threat is 2.Rf5: your rook steps between the black rook and the pawn, and the pawn queens. If 1...Re2+, 2.Re5! blocks the check and 3.Rf5 follows. If the rook takes on f7, the king recaptures and your rook catches the black pawns with 3.Rb4. The hasty 1.f8=Q? only draws: 1...Rxf8 2.Rxf8 Kb3, and the black king with the pawns holds. From Audax6's Lichess study.
key.behind: The white rook is behind the passed pawn, the black rook in front of it. With every step of the pawn the white rook gains room and the black one gets more stuck: White wins.
key.front: The same pieces with the rooks swapped: now it is the white rook that is stuck in front of the pawn. A draw.
key.defend: Now the passed pawn is Black's. The white rook goes behind it and draws; staying in front loses.
key.race: Both rooks are fighting for the square behind the pawn. The white rook has to find the right route to get there first: only one wins.
key.exception: Kramnik vs Beliavsky, 1993: here putting the rook behind the pawn was the losing move. An exception to the rule.
history: When a passed pawn races to promote, the rook works better behind it than in front of it: behind, it gains space with every step the pawn takes; in front, it gets stuck. The rule holds for your own pawn and for your opponent's too. It bears the name of Siegbert Tarrasch (1862–1934), one of the strongest players of his time and such a good teacher that in Germany he was called "the teacher of Germany". He wrote it down in 1914, commenting on a game between Marshall and Lasker at the great St. Petersburg tournament. The rule has famous exceptions, such as Kramnik against Beliavsky in 1993, which is why it is worth understanding why it works rather than just memorising it.
practice: Now the practical challenge: your rook behind the pawn, the black rook in front of it. Bring the king forward and win.
